sources.note: meta.md only (front matter, description); no transcript supplied. No cards.

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Anything that is in the skill or the prompt that you yourself did not write
cards.claim: A model-written skill or prompt only restates what is already in the weights, so letting the model author it adds no useful content and humans should read and write the prompts themselves.
cards.evidence_detail: Stated as a logical argument from experience with model-written skills (e.g. 'always run the tests'); no numbers.
cards.landing: .claude/skills/ authoring rule; CLAUDE.md edits should carry only human-written non-obvious content
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: models are bad at at writing prompts
cards.claim: Prompts are among the most important things to read; if you will not read the code, at least read the prompts, because models write generic prompt filler.
cards.evidence_detail: Opinion backed by the skill-writing anecdote; Aaron's version: print every prompt at each step and read them.
cards.landing: Workflow-tool scripts: dump every prompt in the evidence folder; reviewer step reads the prompt text
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you don't want to have, you know, two hundred new skills, each of which is like one fact
cards.claim: Do not store memory as hundreds of one-fact skills the model must remember to call; skills do not stack well because each invocation injects more user-message context.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex says he does not know how well attention holds with 200 invoked skills and suggests a public 'big skill eval' would be worth building; no data.
cards.landing: Constrains the knowledge-store design and the skills being added under .claude/skills/
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: I don't know if there's an eval for this, but that would be an interesting
cards.claim: There is no known benchmark for how well agents follow instructions when many skills are invoked, or for which skills go stale; he proposes a big-skill eval.
cards.evidence_detail: Open question raised by Dex and agreed by Aaron; no experiment.
cards.landing: Possible cold-resume style test for the skill set; nowhere obvious today
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the answer may not necessarily be to dump a crap ton of facts into the
cards.claim: When agents keep asking the same question, the fix may be one pointer in CLAUDE.md to an existing doc (architecture.md), not new facts.
cards.evidence_detail: BAML repo: 11 sessions by 2 people asked how built-ins are organised; the repo already had architecture.md nobody told agents to read.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md doc map / trimming strategy (pointer instead of prose); knowledge-store design
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: start with the smartest model and the most like you know open open-ended pipeline
cards.claim: Build a pipeline first with the smartest model and open-ended exploration, then distil the patterns that work down to cheaper, more opinionated steps.
cards.evidence_detail: Aaron's run: roughly $100 of Claude Code spend for a report the final pipeline produces for about 50 cents; that run became the golden set.
cards.landing: Workflow authoring: prototype at high effort, then pin cheaper models per step; saved workflow library
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: other
cards.quote: it only kept 60% of the text, but it kept 100% of the data
cards.claim: A cheap classifier pre-filter was tuned against a golden set from the expensive run until recall was 100% of valuable messages while dropping 40% of text.
cards.evidence_detail: Golden-set comparison: 60% of text kept, 100% of golden messages kept; Jev roughly 5% of the bill; about two cents per session; Aaron's, endorsed by Dex.
cards.landing: Verifier/refuter pipelines: cheap screen then strong judge, measured against a frozen golden set
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: other
cards.quote: the weak model, strong model, strong model, weak model, strong model
cards.claim: Alternate weak-model screening with strong-model judging so only survivors reach the expensive model.
cards.evidence_detail: Pipeline shape described by Aaron (classifier filter, group, filter, Opus judge); Dex asks questions and approves.
cards.landing: Effort/model routing for verifiers: screen at low effort, refuter at high only on survivors
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: This is like the vibe eval, right? Like when I eyeball this
cards.claim: Eyeballing outputs, spotting useless ones, and rewriting the question to eliminate them is a legitimate early eval loop, anchored by a golden dataset.
cards.evidence_detail: Describes Aaron's iteration on the tribal-knowledge question for the classifier.
cards.landing: Evidence folders: keep golden set and prior-run outputs beside each workflow
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: other
cards.quote: you're hashing the inputs and then caching that as just a JSON file on disk
cards.claim: Cache each LLM call keyed by input hash so a change to step five reruns without paying for steps one to four.
cards.evidence_detail: Aaron's replay tooling; Dex restates it and the end-to-end-rerun problem; also stores all calls in SQLite via BAML query.
cards.landing: Workflow script helper: input-hash cache and resume for multi-agent scripts
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Okay, so instead of using like the BAML playground to inspect my program
cards.claim: Record every program run in a queryable database an agent can read and let the model vibe a bespoke inspection UI on top, instead of using a generic observability dashboard.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex reacts to Aaron's BAML query demo (SQLite per-run store, dashboard version ten); product-specific to BAML.
cards.landing: Compliance observability: query-able log of phase-routine steps (re-opens skipped 'measurement pipeline')
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you almost need to like run some percentage of your sessions without the memories
cards.claim: To tell whether a memory is stale you would have to run some sessions without it or back-test a new model on old traces, but nobody accepts slower agents for that and long-horizon replay is unreliable.
cards.evidence_detail: Reasoned design discussion; notes that changing the first hundred messages invalidates replaying later recorded user turns.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md pruning criteria; P1 cold-resume trial as an ablation (with/without a section)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: hobbling the model by giving telling it to do things that it already knows how to do
cards.claim: As models improve, instructions that were once needed move into the weights and keep the model hobbled if left in context, so memory needs a staleness check.
cards.evidence_detail: Attributes the 'hobbling' idea to Tariq (Anthropic); no data.
cards.landing: CLAUDE.md trim: periodic removal of rules the current model already follows
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: other
cards.quote: tie each sort of memory to like a place in the codebase or a s or a a region
cards.claim: Tie each memory or context shard to a code region so it loads conditionally and can be checked for staleness when that region changes.
cards.evidence_detail: Aaron's idea for memory health; output was per-region CLAUDE.md files; Dex engages without objection.
cards.landing: Nested/conditional CLAUDE.md per slice (backend/app/features/<x>); knowledge-store design
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: naive. we started with a very naive system
cards.claim: The naive version (user and assistant messages only, tool calls stripped, one Haiku structured-output call) was directionally correct but very bad and needed constant prompt adjustment.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex describing HumanLayer's original context-shard prototype; output was shard, reasoning, citation, session and message id.
cards.landing: Caution for the knowledge-store pilot: first cheap version of a learning pipeline is likely poor
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: where where to find things. You have rules which are like behavioral
cards.claim: Context shards fall into classes: where-to-find-things, behavioural rules (a human asked for an approach), and information that is true but hard to discover from the repo.
cards.evidence_detail: Taxonomy from the generated per-region CLAUDE.md outputs.
cards.landing: Re-sectioning CLAUDE.md into pointers / rules / non-obvious facts
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: other
cards.quote: What I really wanna keep is stuff that is not obvious by reading the code
cards.claim: Judge each candidate memory for whether the agent would see it on opening the file; keep only non-obvious knowledge, or knowledge needing ten file reads to reconstruct, and skip generic advice already in the weights.
cards.evidence_detail: Aaron's judging criteria (tribal knowledge, readability, code-map file-read count); Dex adds the ten-files test.
cards.landing: Admission test for CLAUDE.md lines and knowledge-store entries
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: make it incremental, where like, hey, if I run it again, the final step will
cards.claim: Make a memory pipeline incremental and feed it approved and dismissed memories (with reasons) so it stops regenerating the same suggestions and can propose removals.
cards.evidence_detail: Design sketch with Aaron; fourth pipeline input; not yet built.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store pilot feedback loop; owner approve/dismiss list
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: other
cards.quote: you're not able to make correlations across many sessions
cards.claim: A CLAUDE.md instruction telling agents to write their own memories fails to find patterns across sessions; correlation needs a separate post-hoc job over many sessions.
cards.evidence_detail: Aaron's critique of Cognition's Devin memory approach, with Dex agreeing; no data.
cards.landing: Argues against in-session self-reported memory writes; supports out-of-band session-trace analysis
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: other
cards.quote: you wanna truncate the middle of it
cards.claim: When pruning long messages to save tokens, cut the middle and keep the head and tail; truncating the end loses the conclusion.
cards.evidence_detail: Bug found by Aaron after printing all prompts; Dex agrees.
cards.landing: Output-capping rules for verifier inputs and run_silent-style scripts
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: Gmail came out, they were like, Hey, we're not gonna have folders, we're gonna have labels
cards.claim: Memory should be taggable in multiple places (labels) rather than filed in one hierarchy.
cards.evidence_detail: Analogy offered in discussion of how to store and share memories.
cards.landing: Knowledge-store index design (tags over folders)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #77 Building a Memory Pipeline

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: What's the amount of planning that like maximizes the the or minimizes the expected pain
cards.claim: Choose planning depth by expected pain (chance of rework times its cost), spending effort on hard-to-change things like database tables and skipping easy ones like button colour, with diminishing returns beyond roughly 20 to 30 minutes.
cards.evidence_detail: Illustrative curve: two-sentence YOLO about 50% rework, detailed spec 10%; numbers are illustrative, not measured.
cards.landing: Phase routine plan depth per phase; risk-scaled planning (migrations/money vs UI)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the percentage of PRs that met that policy shot up from like 10% to like 80%
cards.claim: A rule that small PRs not touching core modules may merge without human review pushed engineers to split risky parts out; qualifying PRs rose from about 10% to 80%.
cards.evidence_detail: Second-hand from one founder; policy details not known to Dex.
cards.landing: Reviewer scope by touched-path risk; PR splitting rule (migrations, money, dispatcher separate)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: other
cards.quote: does this code do this? And it basically just turns everything into a Boolean
cards.claim: Per-file ownership rules mixing regexes and LLM-judged booleans can hold a changed file for a named human until they approve it (e.g. new env-var read, new S3 dependency, persisted or serialized state).
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's in-house tool; Dex asks about the expression language, agrees; Zach says risk-tiered review makes sense.
cards.landing: Mechanical gate for migrations/models.py, money columns and dispatcher paths (re-opens skipped hooks/pre-commit gate)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you can't just let them write all the code
cards.claim: Fresh from the transcript: Dex says the worth of the factory loop is that AI barely changes the shape of it (implement, review, QA), and whether QA runs before or after review depends on which step is more expensive.
cards.evidence_detail: Brief aside; he and Zach had swapped the order of review and QA on the whiteboard.
cards.landing: Ordering of verifier steps by cost (cheap checks first) in phase routine
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: start with the thing you have and make it a little bit better every day
cards.claim: Hill-climb from the current process against a defined notion of better rather than redesigning the whole process around a factory; a redesign in a hole risks building what nobody wants.
cards.evidence_detail: Advice he says he has given many times; no data.
cards.landing: Phase routine rollout: incremental adoption after P1 cold-resume trial, not wholesale
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: other
cards.quote: record everything that's happening in your factory, which to me is a prerequisite
cards.claim: Recording every agent run is the prerequisite for improvement; online evals over sampled runs (e.g. share writing redundant tests, split by model) and an automation index counting human steering per PR turn vibes into measures.
cards.evidence_detail: Zach (Warp) demo of default factory metrics: DORA, cost by engineer and stage, steering count; Dex reacts that this replaces 'Opus writes too many tests' vibes.
cards.landing: Compliance evidence: count human steering and skipped routine steps from session traces (re-opens measurement pipeline)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: time wasted trying to learn how to use the system, right?
cards.claim: Detect 'relearning' in traces (an agent trying six commands to run tests) and feed it into a skill or CLAUDE.md fix; ties to the memory-pipeline episode.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex proposes the metric; Zach says it would be an online eval feeding skill improvement.
cards.landing: Skill/CLAUDE.md candidates mined from repeated failed commands; knowledge-store input
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: you now have an RL environment and then you can replay other things on it
cards.claim: A recorded run with model, environment, starting SHA and base image saved is a replayable benchmark; the hard part is stopping the agent from seeing the finished commit or landed PR.
cards.evidence_detail: Zach describes Warp feature and the cheating problem; Dex adds the RL-environment framing.
cards.landing: Replay-based tests for the harness (cold-resume style) and for effort-level comparison
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: mapping skill used to and version of the skill used to like the sentiment of the session
cards.claim: One 300-engineer factory maps skill and skill version used to session sentiment on analytics dashboards to improve base prompts.
cards.evidence_detail: Second-hand report from a person Dex talked to; no numbers.
cards.landing: Skill versioning plus per-skill outcome tracking
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: other
cards.quote: define your factory in code. So think of like Terraform
cards.claim: Define the agents, skills, MCPs, models and where they run declaratively so the factory can be branched, tested and have agents propose diffs against it from patterns of failed runs.
cards.evidence_detail: Zach (Warp) product pitch; Dex and Vaibhav accept the shape as established.
cards.landing: Saved workflow library as versioned files in repo (.claude/workflows) with agent-proposed diffs
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: people who work with a lot of agents should probably slow down
cards.claim: Running ten agents in parallel reduces quality and slows everything; one or two things at a time, and pairing helps keep focus.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex relays a Tariq (Anthropic) thread and adds his own pairing experience; no data.
cards.landing: One phase per session / limit parallel refuters and worktrees
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: the more you can get people to watch each other work, the faster everybody learns
cards.claim: Public, multiplayer prompting spreads techniques quickly, but it needs psychological safety and a culture of working in the open or adoption stalls.
cards.evidence_detail: Experience with customer teams; no numbers.
cards.landing: Owner view and decisions journal visible in the draft PR
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: take the thing we just built and reverse engineer it into a P R D
cards.claim: Vibe a prototype, then reverse-engineer it into a spec and have the real design done properly; Vaibhav's variant rewrites the spec after implementation and redoes the code from it.
cards.evidence_detail: Dex does it for prototypes; Vaibhav does spec to implementation to spec to implementation in two loops and says code is better; no numbers.
cards.landing: Phase routine option: throwaway spike then re-plan; decisions journal capture
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate

cards.author: Dex
cards.quote: fundamentally, you cannot have a factory if you have two separate orgs
cards.claim: Product and engineering must co-own the whole loop through customer outcome; silos and unwillingness to give up turf, not engineering, are why factories fail (Dex adds the Hashimoto Vault story that refusing a customer can make them fix their culture).
cards.evidence_detail: Vaibhav's takeaway built on Dex's comment; Dex adds the anecdote.
cards.landing: nowhere obvious (single-owner project)
cards.inventory_ref: (B) October 2026 — AI That Works #78 Software Factory Debate
